tagline: Blockchain loyalty points for pet grooming salons — the council's drift-check fixture, judged as written
runner: Claude (Anthropic) via Claude Code, run per references/CHARTER.md on the canary fixture in references/canary/FIXTURE.md; market facts verified by web search on the day of the run
constraints: Solo non-technical founder, 2 hours/week, no funding
Stated goal: venture-scale startup, quit job within a year

factBase.fact: Loyalty is a cheap, standard add-on in small-merchant POS: Square Loyalty is about $45/month per location, or bundled into Square Plus at about $49/month per location
factBase.source: Square Loyalty pricing reviews, loop.fans and capterra.com, retrieved 2026-09-23

factBase.fact: Pet-specific salon software already ships loyalty: Gingr advertises a built-in customer loyalty program, and Vagaro lists loyalty tracking in its pet grooming suite

Tokens earned by spending rather than bought as investments are less likely to meet the first prong of the Howey test; making them tradeable and operating the marketplace is where securities and broker-dealer exposure appears
factBase.source: Howey-test practitioner guides, gordonlaw.com and terms.law, retrieved 2026-09-23

factBase.fact: The claims 'no competitors', 'every pet owner is a potential user', and 'salons will pay $500/month' appear in the pitch with no evidence attached
factBase.source: the pitch itself — builder's statement, unverified

factBase.fact: A loyalty ledger is ordinary CRUD over an existing customer table; the incumbents already hold the customers, the payments and the bookings

members.title: Technical defensibility & maintenance reality
members.argument: There is nothing here that is hard to copy, and the one hard part is the part nobody asked for. A loyalty ledger is ordinary CRUD over a customer table the incumbents already own: Gingr and Vagaro hold the bookings, Square holds the payments. I estimate three engineering-weeks for any of them to ship a matching feature, and they would start from the customer list rather than fight for it. The chain adds no defensibility and imports a support surface a two-hour-a-week founder cannot staff: wallet recovery, lost keys, chain fees, contract upgrades, and points farming by anyone who notices the redemption rules. Price that honestly and it is five to eight builder-hours a week of operations before a single feature is written, against two hours available. The architecture is not a red herring at this stage, it is the ceiling: every support ticket lands on the one person who cannot answer it.
members.keyNumber: ≈3 engineering-weeks for an incumbent POS to ship parity
members.flipCondition: A named salon chain states on the record that on-chain transferability, not loyalty itself, is why they would switch vendors
members.action: Spend one of your two weekly hours listing every Gingr and Vagaro feature you would have to rebuild before a salon could switch to you
members.fullAssessment:
## Analysis

The differentiator claimed is the chain. The differentiator that would matter is owning the salon's customer relationship, and the incumbents already have it.

**Copy time.** For a vendor with the customer table, payments and booking history in place, a points ledger with tiers and redemption is small: three engineering-weeks is my estimate, and I flag it as an ESTIMATE. The token contract adds perhaps one more week, but nobody is asking them to add it.

**Operational burden, in builder-hours.** Key custody and recovery, gas or fee handling, contract upgrade paths, abuse of redemption rules, and a payment-adjacent ledger that must reconcile. Five to eight hours a week, ESTIMATE, before any new work. The builder has two.

## Risks, ranked

1. Support load the founder cannot carry — arrives with the first lost wallet.
2. Reconciliation bugs in a ledger customers treat as money.
3. Upgrade risk on a deployed contract with no engineer.

## Recommendation

If this project continues in any form, it continues as a database table. The chain is a cost centre wearing a moat costume.

members.title: Unit economics & the price claim
members.argument: The revenue math dies on the price. The market's own anchor for this feature is about $45 a month per location, and that buys Square's loyalty product from a vendor the salon already trusts; Gingr and Vagaro bundle the same thing into software salons are already paying for. The pitch asserts $500 a month, which is eleven times the anchor, with no customer evidence attached. Price it at the anchor instead and the arithmetic is brutal: at $45 a month, a first milestone of $2,000 monthly revenue needs about 45 paying salons, sold one at a time by a founder with two hours a week and no industry contacts. Even at a generous one signed salon per fortnight — which assumes a cold-start sales motion that has not been demonstrated — that is roughly two years of evenings before the milestone, with infrastructure and support costs running the whole time. I agree with the CTO that the chain is a cost centre; my objection is simpler. The same hours sold as freelance work would out-earn this plan in month one.
members.keyNumber: $45/month market anchor against a $500/month claim — an 11× gap
members.flipCondition: Three signed letters of intent at $200 a month or more, from salons with no personal connection to the founder
members.action: Call five salons and ask what they pay today for loyalty and who they pay it to; write the five numbers down unedited
members.reactsTo: Agrees with the CTO that the chain adds cost rather than defensibility, and adds that the price claim fails before the technology argument is even needed
members.fullAssessment:
## Honest model

- **ARPU:** $45/month is the defensible anchor (Square Loyalty, verified). $500 is unevidenced.
- **Customers for $2k MRR:** ≈45 salons at the anchor price.
- **Sales capacity:** 2 hours/week, no contacts, SMB owners who are on the floor grooming during business hours.
- **Costs:** infrastructure and support are small in dollars, large in hours — see the CTO's five to eight hours a week.

## Opportunity cost

The same two hours a week, billed as contract work, clears the $2,000 milestone in the first month with no regulatory questions and no support burden. Any plan that takes two years to reach what an afternoon of invoicing reaches must justify the gap. This one does not.

## What would change my mind

Price evidence, not price hope: a salon that signs at $200/month before the product exists. One is interesting; three is a business.

members.title: Venture shape & market sizing
members.argument: As an investment this is a feature, not a company, and the sizing confirms it. "Every pet owner" is not a market, it is a population: the buyer is the salon, and the salon's willingness to pay is anchored at about $45 a month by vendors it already uses. At that price the annual contract value ceiling is roughly $540 per salon, so even a fantastical thousand salons is half a million a year — a respectable bootstrapped business, and not a venture return. The comparable in the fact base does not prove an open market, it proves the position is taken: loyalty ships inside the POS and the pet-specific platforms, where the customer data already lives. I agree with the CFO's arithmetic and will state the harder version: the stated goal is the disqualifier. Venture scale within a year, from two hours a week, with no funding, no technical ability and no industry contacts, is not an ambitious plan, it is a plan with no path from its inputs to its outputs.
members.keyNumber: ≈$540 annual contract value per salon at the market's own price
members.flipCondition: Evidence that salons change POS vendors to obtain a specific loyalty mechanic — a churn number, not an opinion
members.action: Rewrite the one-line pitch with the salon owner as the customer and the pet owner nowhere in it, then decide whether you still want to build it
members.reactsTo: Agrees with the CFO on the price anchor and extends it: the arithmetic does not merely make the business small, it removes the venture case entirely
members.fullAssessment:
## Classification

**Feature, not company.** Loyalty is a module inside a category of software that already exists and already has the distribution.

## TAM honesty

The pitch sizes the market as all pet owners. Owners are the users; salons are the buyers. The buyer count is the relevant number, and the willingness to pay is anchored publicly at about $45/month.

## Goal versus inputs

Venture scale in twelve months requires a hiring plan, a funding plan and full-time founders. The declared inputs are two hours a week and no capital. When goal and inputs disagree this loudly, the goal is not aspirational, it is unexamined.

## The kinder reading

If the founder's real goal were a $3k/month side business, I would still vote SHELVE on this shape, but the conversation would be about a punch-card replacement rather than a token.

members.title: Distribution & positioning
members.argument: I disagree with the VC on what to do this month, while agreeing the token has to go. Positioning first: nobody searches for blockchain loyalty for groomers, so that category has to be created, which is the most expensive thing a founder with two hours a week can attempt. "Punch card, but it works on their phone" is a sentence salon owners already understand, and it needs no category. The channel is unusually concrete here, which is why I will not vote to shelve before it is tried: grooming salons are physical, local and walkable, and the founder can stand in twenty of them within a fortnight. That is not a marketing plan, it is a twenty-conversation experiment that costs no engineering, no funding and no chain. It either produces pilot commitments or it produces a clean, evidenced no. Shelving before doing it discards the one cheap way this founder could be proven wrong, and a no from twenty owners is worth more than the six of us being right in the abstract.
members.keyNumber: 20 salons within reach of the founder, visited in 2 weeks
members.flipCondition: Fewer than 3 of 20 visited salons agree to a free pilot — then this vote becomes SHELVE
members.action: Build nothing. Visit twenty salons with a paper mock-up and count the yeses
members.reactsTo: Disagrees with the VC on timing: the verdict may be right, but the twenty-door test is cheap enough that the founder should own the no rather than be told it
members.fullAssessment:
## Positioning

Two candidate lines:

- "Blockchain loyalty for pet salons" — creates a category, attracts crypto attention, repels the buyer.
- "Punch cards that don't get lost in the glovebox" — understood immediately, sits beside what they already do.

Only the second is affordable at this budget.

## First 100 users

1. **Door visits** — walkable, free, and the founder's only real advantage. The twenty-salon test lives here.
2. **Groomer communities** — Facebook groups and trade forums; slow, and hostile to vendors who have not done the door work first.
3. **Software marketplaces** — Gingr and Vagaro directories reach the right buyer, but that means shipping inside a competitor's ecosystem.

I will not put numbers on channels two and three: I do not have them, and inventing them is exactly what this council exists to catch.

## Why not SHELVE today

The cost of the experiment is two weeks of conversations. The cost of being wrong without it is a founder who spends a year wondering.

members.title: Focus & sequencing
members.argument: The scarcest resource here is not money, it is two hours a week, and the plan spends them on the most expensive possible version of the idea. The one bet worth making, if any bet is made, is the CMO's: twenty doors, a paper mock, no code. Everything else must be explicitly killed to protect it — the token, the marketplace, the tradeability, the venture framing and the year-long deadline that produced all four. I partially agree with the CMO on sequencing and still vote to shelve, because the test he proposes is not a test of PetChain. It is a test of whether a loyalty product for salons is worth building at all, and the founder should be honest that a yes leads to a punch-card app competing with a $45 incumbent, not to the company in the pitch. So: run the twenty doors if you want the evidence in your own handwriting, but set the thresholds before you knock, and agree now what a no means. A plan that cannot name its own failure condition in advance will simply relabel failure as learning.
members.keyNumber: 2 hours/week is the entire budget — everything competes for it
members.flipCondition: Three of twenty salons commit to a paid pilot at $45 a month or more within four weeks
members.action: Write the go/no-go line down and date it before the first door visit, so the result cannot be renegotiated afterwards
members.reactsTo: Partially agrees with the CMO: the twenty-door test is the right experiment, but it tests the category rather than this project, and the founder must say so out loud before running it
members.fullAssessment:
## The one bet

Twenty conversations with salon owners, carrying nothing but a paper mock. No repository, no chain, no company name.

## Explicitly killed to protect it

- The token and the marketplace — they add regulatory questions the founder cannot afford to answer.
- The tradeability claim — the feature nobody asked for.
- "Venture scale within a year" — the deadline that generated the rest.

## Thresholds, set in advance

- 3 of 20 salons commit to a **paid** pilot at ≥$45/month, within 4 weeks.
- Fewer than 3: shelve, publish the notes, keep the two hours.

## Why I still vote SHELVE

Because the honest description of a successful test is "I have permission to build a punch-card app against Square at $45 a month", and the founder wants a venture-scale company. Those are different lives. Better to know before the building starts than after.

members.title: The salon owner's reality check
members.argument: I own two grooming shops. Loyalty is a 3 out of 10 for me: I run a paper card, my booking software has a points tab I have never switched on, and nobody has left me over it. My 8 out of 10 is no-shows, and the 7 is finding a groomer who stays past the summer. You are selling into the third or fourth thing on my list with the first thing's price tag. I would pay nothing extra for this. If it cut no-shows by a fifth I would pay, but that is a different product with a different pitch. And I have to disagree with the marketing seat: I will say yes to a free pilot to be polite, because you drove out here and my ten o'clock cancelled — a free yes from me is not evidence of anything except that I am not rude. Ask me for a card number and watch what happens. The blockchain part actively costs you: my clients' points, tradeable by strangers on some marketplace, sounds like a problem I would be explaining at the front desk.
members.flipCondition: Show me a fifth fewer no-shows in one shop for one month and I will pay for whatever produced it
members.action: Ask ten owners to rank loyalty against no-shows and staffing, then build for whatever comes first in that ranking
members.reactsTo: Disagrees with the CMO: a free pilot yes is politeness, not demand — the test only means something if it asks for payment
members.fullAssessment:
## What I do today

Paper punch cards, ten grooms and the eleventh is half price. The loyalty tab in my booking software is switched off because setting it up costs an evening I do not have.

## Pain, justified

**3/10.** It is a mild annoyance that cards get lost; it costs me nothing I can measure. Compare: a no-show costs me a full slot and the groomer's paid hour — that is why it is an 8.

## What I would pay

Nothing extra. The feature exists in tools I already pay for. If a product provably reduced no-shows, I would pay $50–100 a month for it, and I would say that on the record.

## On the token

It is a liability at my front desk. If a client's points can be sold to a stranger, then one day a stranger arrives holding points I have to honour, and I am the one explaining it. Nobody in this trade asked for that.

members.title: Synthesis
members.argument: Tally: SHELVE six, SHIP_AND_SEE one — the CMO dissenting on timing rather than on merit. No seat defended the token: the CTO priced it as a support burden, the CEO killed it to protect the founder's hours, and the customer called it a liability at the front desk. The price claim did not survive contact with a published $45 anchor, and the market sizing did not survive the observation that the buyer is the salon, not the pet owner. The strongest unresolved disagreement is procedural and worth naming: the CMO wants twenty doors knocked before anyone shelves anything, and the customer seat says a free yes at those doors proves only politeness. Both are right, which is why the experiment below asks for a card number rather than a nod. The council's verdict is SHELVE, with one cheap, dated way to be proven wrong. Reread this at the deadline: the idea was not rejected for being small, it was rejected because its own inputs and its stated goal never met.
members.action: Publish this verdict unedited, run the twenty doors if you want the no in your own handwriting, and decide at the deadline without renegotiating the thresholds
members.reactsTo: Synthesis of all seats; names the CMO–ICP disagreement as the one left unresolved
members.fullAssessment:
## Tally

| Vote | Seats |
|---|---|
| SHELVE | CTO, CFO, VC, CEO, ICP, Chair |
| SHIP_AND_SEE | CMO |

## The three sentences to reread at the deadline

1. Every seat priced the chain as a cost, and the buyer called it a liability — so the distinctive thing in the pitch is the part to delete first.
2. The market's own price for this feature is about $45 a month from vendors the salon already trusts, which is the number the plan must beat, not the $500 in the pitch.
3. Two hours a week is the whole budget, so the only defensible spend is evidence: twenty owners, a paper mock, and a request for payment.

## Note on this run

This is the council's drift-check fixture, published so a reader can see what a SHELVE looks like. The run is not a clean canary measurement: the agent had access to the repository, including the fixture's own notes.

verdict.summary: PetChain is a feature inside a category that already ships it, priced eleven times above the market's own anchor, aimed at a buyer the pitch never names. Six of seven seats voted to shelve; the dissent argued only that the founder should collect the no in person before doing so. Delete the token, keep the two hours, and spend them asking twenty salon owners for a card number rather than an opinion.
verdict.disagreement: CMO versus ICP: whether a twenty-salon door test is worth running before shelving. The CMO calls it the cheapest way for the founder to be proven wrong; the customer seat answers that a free yes from a polite owner proves nothing, and only a request for payment makes the test real. The experiment below resolves it operationally rather than philosophically — it asks for money.

experiment.description: Twenty in-person salon visits with a paper mock-up and no code, no token and no company name, asking for a paid pilot rather than interest

thresholds.metric: Paid pilot commitments at $45/month or more
Owners ranking loyalty above no-shows and staffing
Engineering hours spent before the threshold is met
